question: Which of the following statements best describes the arterial blood supply for the extraocular muscles?

options.A: The medial and lateral rectus muscles carry the bulk of the blood supply to the anterior segment of the eye.
options.B: The lateral muscular branch of the ophthalmic artery supplies the lateral rectus, superior rectus, superior oblique, and levator muscles
options.C: The medial muscular branch of the ophthalmic artery supplies the lateral rectus, superior rectus, superior oblique, and levator muscles
options.D: the infraorbital artery partially supplies the superior oblique and lateral rectus muscles

explanation: Each rectus muscle has 1 to 3 anterior ciliary arteries which are branches of the muscular arteries which themselves are branches of the ophthalmic artery. The lateral muscular branch supplies the lateral rectus, superior rectus, superior oblique, and levator palpebrae muscles. The medial muscular branch supplies the inferior rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique muscles. Also, the infraorbital artery partially supplies the inferior oblique and inferior rectus muscles.

question: Including active muscle and tendon, what is the shortest overall extraocular muscle?
explanation: See Table 2-1 in the BCSC Pediatrics book. The active muscular portions of the medial rectus, superior rectus, lateral rectus, inferior rectus, and levator are 40 mm. The superior oblique has an active muscular portion of 32 mm. The inferior oblique has an active muscular portion of 37 mm. The muscles with the longest tendons are the superior oblique and levator with 26 mm and 14-20 mm, respectively. This makes the superior oblique the longest overall muscle. Because of its small tendon length (1 mm) the smallest overall muscle is the inferior oblique.

question: All of the following are TRUE regarding the innervation of the extraocular muscles EXCEPT

options.A: CN IV should not be affected by a retrobulbar block because it lies outside the muscle cone
options.B: The nerves to the recti and superior oblique muscles are two-thirds of the distance from the origin to the insertion
options.C: Injury to the nerve to the inferior oblique muscle during a inferotemporal retrobulbar block may lead to pupillary abnormalities
options.D: The nerve innervating the inferior oblique enters the lateral portion of this muscle

explanation: Actually, the nerves to the recti and superior oblique muscles are one-third of the distance from the muscle origin to insertion. Damage to these nerves during anterior segment surgery is unlikely. But a long needle or instrument (>26mm) posterior to the muscle insertion to cause injury to the nerve. (FYI, a Atkinson retrobulbar needle is 40 mm long) The nerve supplying the inferior oblique enters the muscle laterally, when it crosses the inferior rectus muscle. Since the parasympathetic innervation to the pupillary sphincter travels with the nerve of the inferior oblique, injury to the nerve of the inferior oblique muscle can result in a permanently dilated pupil. This can occur during orbit surgery or from a inferotemporal retrobulbar block. Cranial nerve IV is outside the muscle cone so the function of the superior oblique is not usually affected by a retrobulbar block. But any muscle can be reached by a retrobulbar needle and injection of local anesthetic can cause injury or the needle can directly injure the muscle.

question: All of the following statements regarding the inferior oblique muscle are true EXCEPT:

options.A: It originates from the ethmoid bone
options.B: It passes inferior (i.e. farther from the globe) to the inferior rectus muscle
options.C: It inserts near the macula underneath the lateral rectus muscle
options.D: It is innervated by the inferior division of CN III

explanation: The inferior oblique actually originates from the periosteum of the maxillary bone. All of the other statements are true regarding the inferior oblique muscle. One fact that is confusing is that the inferior oblique passes inferior to the inferior rectus muscle. In other words, the inferior oblique is farther away (or external) to the inferior rectus. The superior oblique muscle also passes inferior to the superior rectus muscle. However in that case, the superior oblique is "underneath" (i.e. closer to the globe) the superior rectus. Comments: - oBliques go Below.

explanation: See Table 2-1 in the BCSC Pediatrics book. The active muscular portions of the medial rectus, superior rectus, lateral rectus, inferior rectus, and levator are 40 mm. question: The superior and inferior recti muscles form an angle of HOW MANY DEGREES with the visual axis of the eye?
explanation: The vertical recti muscles course laterally from the annulus of Zinn forming an angle of 23 degrees with the visual axis of the eye. This contrasts the oblique muscles which form an angle of 51 degrees with the visual axis of the eye. PHYSIOLOGY.

question: Which of the following statements is true regarding central and peripheral fusion?

options.A: The area near the fovea has a small receptive field and thus objects can be of dissimilar size and shape and still be seen singly
options.B: The area near the fovea has a large receptive field and thus objects can be of dissimilar size and shape and still be seen singly
options.C: The area in the peripheral retina has a small receptive field and thus objects can be of dissimilar size and shape and still be seen singly
options.D: The area in the peripheral retina has a large receptive field and thus objects can be of dissimilar size and shape and still be seen singly

explanation: The area near the fovea has small receptive fields; therefore, objects need to be very similar in terms of size and shape to be fused properly ("central fusion"). Conversely, the peripheral retina has a large receptive field; thus objects can be more dissimilar in size and shape and still be fused ("peripheral fusion").

question: You are assessing the primary action of the superior rectus muscle. What would you tell this patient to do to maximize this muscle's primary action?

options.A: abduct your eye 23 degrees from primary position
options.B: abduct your eye 67 degrees from primary position
options.C: adduct your eye 23 degrees from primary position
options.D: adduct your eye 67 degrees from primary position

explanation: The primary action of the superior rectus is elevation. Since the superior rectus inserts onto the globe at an angle of 23 degrees from the primary visual axis, abduction of 23 degrees will align the visual axis with the muscle axis. The net effect will be maximal elevation of the eye. If the patient could adduct 67 degrees (which is not physiologically possible), then the superior rectus would be a pure intorter (i.e. its secondary action).

question: You are contemplating performing bilateral medial rectus recessions on a 45- year-old patient with long-standing esotropia. During the course of your pre- operative exam, you determine that he has anomalous retinal correspondence (ARC). Which of the following may happen shortly after your planned strabismus surgery?
explanation: If a patient has developed anomalous retinal correspondence (ARC) as a result of strabismus, then he maintains single vision by projecting the images of an object onto different retinal areas between the two eyes. If the deviation is corrected fully with surgery, then the ARC may persist leading to "paradoxical diplopia." In the esotrope, this would lead to CROSSED diplopia. This is paradoxical because usually in esotropes, one would experience UNCROSSED diplopia. Think of it this way: a patient measures ET, but the patient has ARC so he himself is perceiving less ET than he measures. When we do surgery to fix the measured ET, the patient himself is now feeling XT (because he was perceiving less ET than he measured pre-op, so now he is perceiving "over-correction"), and hence post-op for this patient, he will experience CROSSED diplopia as if he is XT. One can also simulate crossed and uncrossed diplopia to aid in understanding of this concept. One experiences uncrossed diplopia when one is eSotropic, and one experiences crossed diplopia when one is eXotropic. To simulate eSotropia, grab a pen in one hand and hold it in front of you with your arm extended, then place your other hand's index finger approximately half distance from your pen and your nose (ok to be closer to your nose). Focus on your index finger (this is you in convergence or eSotropia). Now your pen in the background is outside of Panum's area and should be seen as 2 separate images (one on the left and another one on the right. Don't worry if you don't see the diplopic pen yet. Now close your left eye, the pen image on the left disappears! Then open your left eye and close your right eye, the pen image on the right disappears! You have just experienced UNCROSSED diplopia from eSotropia. Similarly, to simulate eXotropia, perform the same arrangement. Now, instead of focusing on your index finger, focus on your pen to start with (this is you in divergence or eXotropia). Your index finger is outside of Panum's area and should be doubled. Again, don't worry if you don't see it yet. Now close your left eye, the index finger on the right disappears! Now open your left eye and close the right eye, the index finger on the left disappears! This is CROSSED diplopia from eXotropia. The reason for the above phenomenon is as follows: in eSotropia, the eyeball is turned inward, so the fovea is moved outward, away from the nose or temporally. An image/light that is coming in from straight ahead is going to fall nasal to the fovea (remember the fovea is moved outward or temporally in eSotropia). But then the nasal side of the retina perceives the temporal side of the visual field. So the image is perceived as coming from the temporal side of the visual field. So an eSotropic eye sees the image displaced temporally and is UNCROSSED. Now the opposite situation occurs for eXotropia. The eyeball is turned outward, so the fovea is moved inward or toward the nose or nasally. An image/light coming from straight ahead is falling temporal to the fovea (again, remember the fovea is now inward or nasal), and thus the perceived image is the nasal side of the visual field. So in eXotropia, the diplopia image is perceived as displaced nasally and is CROSSED (like a X).

question: You are reviewing a 48-year-old patient's chart who has the notation "30 PD X(T)" noted in his chart. The patient has 40 sec arc on stereopsis testing. T he patient does not complain of any double vision at any time in the past. Which of the following types of suppression does he likely manifest?
explanation: Suppression is a sensory adaption in strabismus. When an eye is deviated, a normal person should be experiencing two different images on the two foveas (visual confusion = seeing two different images overlapped) and/or the same image on the fovea of one eye and on the peripheral retina or some extrafoveal region of the other eye (diplopia = seeing the same image in two different places). In order to avoid visual confusion or diplopia, suppression occurs. When an eye is deviated, in order to avoid visual confusion, central suppression occurs. Central suppression prevents the two different images on the two fovea from reaching the brain, thereby eliminating visual confusion. Central suppression is present almost all of the time, in young and old. This is the reason why we do not encounter visual confusion very often in clinic and the reason why adults with acquired new-onset strabismus complain of diplopia (see below) and not confusion. When an eye is deviated, peripheral suppression is suppression of the image falling on the peripheral retina in the deviated eye corresponding to the image falling on the fovea of the fixating eye. Peripheral suppression is for elimination of diplopia, and is only developed in an immature visual system. Adults with acquired new-onset strabismus will always complain of diplopia while a long-standing strabismus developed during childhood that decompensates or manifests in adulthood will not complain of diplopia. The patient here has intermittent exotropia. He has excellent stereoacuity when his eyes are in the non-deviated state. Also, he does not complain of any double vision. These suggest that he must be utilizing some suppression when his eyes are deviated but the suppression is absent when the eyes are aligned. This type of suppression is called facultative suppression since it only occurs when the eyes are deviated. Obligatory suppression is suppression that is present even when the eyes are aligned or deviated -- i.e. it is suppression that is present all of the time. Obligatory suppression leads to decrease in vision, an example of which is amblyopia.

question: Which of the following statements best defines the visual axis of the eye?

options.A: A line that best approximates the line passing through the optical centers of the cornea, lens, and fovea
options.B: An imaginary line connecting the fixation point and the fovea
options.C: The imaginary line perpendicular to the cornea and passing through the midpoint of the pupil
options.D: The imaginary line that is perpendicular to both the cornea and fovea

explanation:
"A" describes the "optical axis" of the eye. "C" describes the "pupillary axis" of the eye. 
"D" does not describe any axis of the eye.

question: You are performing an inferior oblique weakening procedure on a patient with congenital esotropia who has concomitant inferior oblique overaction. What would be the effect of this surgery on this muscle's tertiary action?
explanation:
Only the vertical recti and oblique muscles have tertiary actions. Adduction is the 
tertiary action for the superior and inferior recti while abduction is the tertiary action for 
the obliques.

question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding "Panum's area of single binocular vision"?

options.A: A 3-dimensional object is seen singly if the front of the object is within Panum's area
options.B: A 3-dimensional object is seen singly if the back of the object is within Panum's area
options.C: A 3-dimensional object is seen as a double image if any part of it falls outside of Panum's area
options.D: A 3-dimensional object is seen as a double image only if *all* of it falls outside of Panum's area

explanation: Panum's area of single binocular vision describes the area in space where an object can fall mathematically on disparate retinal areas, but still be seen as a single object. The *entire* object must fall within this space to be seen as a single object.

question: You perform a Worth-4-Dot test on a 4-year-old boy. He is wearing red-green glasses with the red lens over the right eye and the green lens over the left eye. At a distance of 10 ft, the child reports seeing 2 dots, and at a distance of 2 ft, the child reports seeing 4 dots. What does this child have and does he have amblyopia?

options.A: Monofixation syndrome with OD being the amblyopic eye
options.B: Monofixation syndrome with OS being the amblyopic eye
options.C: Normal response on the W4D test but has dense amblyopia in OD
options.D: Normal response on the W4D test but has dense amblyopia in OS

explanation: The Worth-4-Dot test can be used to check for monofixation syndrome and help with amblyopia testing in a child who may not know letters or be cooperative with visual acuity testing. With the red lens over OD and the green lens over OS, the W4D test is checked first at distance. If the response is 4 dots, then it is a normal response. If the response is 2 dots, then the OD is dominant. If the response is 3 dots, then OS is dominant. Seeing 2- or 3- dots means that there is a suppression scotoma. Next, the test is performed at near. If the response is the same, then there is a large suppression scotoma, i.e. dense amblyopia. If the response becomes 4 dots, then this suggests that the image has fallen outside of the central small suppression scotoma, commonly seen in monofixation syndrome.

question: A 3-year-old patient is referred for a failed vision screening at his pediatrician’s office. Visual acuity is 20/25 OD and 20/125 OS (method: matching single bracketed HOTV). Examination is significant for hypermetropic anisometropia of +2.00 sph OD and +5.00 sph OS. In refractive correction, there is no improvement in measured visual acuity. Based on the method of visual acuity testing, is the visual acuity in the amblyopic eye accurately, under-, or over- estimated?

options.A: Over-estimated, as single optotypes are utilized
options.B: Over-estimated, as linear Snellen was not utilized
options.C: Accurate, as bracketed single optotypes are utilized
options.D: Under-estimated as a 3-year-old likely does not know the letters H, O, T, V

explanation: One of the findings associated with amblyopia is the phenomenon of contour interaction or crowding phenomenon. When single optotypes are utilized, the visual acuity is often better than when linear or bracketed optotypes are used. In this specific case, bracketed single HOTV are used and therefore the visual acuity is likely accurately reflected. The child matches the optotypes on the distance screen to a card and therefore, he does not need to be familiar or verbalize the letters.

question: You are speaking with a medical student friend who just gave birth to a healthy full-term baby 2 weeks ago. Your friend is concerned because her baby does not seem to make eye contact or react with facial expressions. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Do not worry. Your baby will not make eye contact with you until she is at least 4 months old.
options.B: I will perform a dilated eye exam to rule out ocular causes of her poor vision.
options.C: You should consider obtaining neuroimaging to exclude a brain lesion causing her poor vision.
options.D: Do not worry. Your baby will not make eye contact with you until she is at least 6 weeks old.

explanation:
The normal baby will begin to make eye contact and react with facial expressions at 
approximately 6 weeks of age.

question: Which of the following eye movements are typically absent at birth?
explanation: STRABISMUS/AMBLYOPIA.

question: Which of the following is an example of optical penalization?

options.A: Prescribing a high plus lens to the sound eye (non-amblyopic eye) in a patient without refractive error (non-amblyopic eye) for amblyopia therapy
options.B: Performing photorefractive keratectomy to correct extreme refractive error in an amblyopic eye
options.C: Prescribing bilateral over-minus lenses in a patient with poorly controlled intermittent exotropia
options.D: Prescribing a high minus contact lens to the sound eye (non-amblyopic eye) in a patient without refractive error (non-amblyopic eye) for amblyopia therapy

explanation: "Optical penalization" involves applying something to the sound eye to potentially augment amblyopia therapy. Prescription of excessive plus lenses or a diffusing filter (Bangerter foil) serves the purpose of fogging the non-amblyopic eye. For children or parents who will cannot tolerate or accept patching therapy, optic penalization may be more acceptable way to amblyopia therapy. (BCSC Peds book, Chapter on amblyopia, Sub-section on occlusion and penalization). Giving a high plus lens (e.g. +13.00) inducing blur is the reason behind optical penalization. A child's ability to accommodate is significant, so giving a weak plus lens or minus lens is not effective as the patient will be able to accommodate through it. A contact lens can optically penalize the sound eye (choice D), but the risk of infection associated with a contact lens is high in an essentially monocular patient. Another way of using optical penalization is for treatment of DVD. We sometimes use optical penalization to change fixation preference so that the patient uses the DVD eye (the non-preferred eye, hence manifest DVD) to fixate. This blurs the vision in the preferred eye and ameliorates a noticeable unilateral or asymmetric DVD in the non- preferred eye. Prescribing over-minus lenses (choice C) is not a treatment for amblyopia, but increases accommodative convergence and may improve control of intermittent exotropia in some patients. Performing photorefractive keratectomy (choice B) on a highly anisometropic amblyopia eye is sometimes performed to improve vision in cases where other forms of refractive correction and penalization therapy have been ineffective.

question: All of the following are possible interventions to prevent symptomatic superior oblique palsy during the treatment of Brown syndrome EXCEPT:

options.A: careful handling of the intermuscular septum during tenotomy
options.B: complete tenectomy of the posterior portion of the superior oblique tendon
options.D: sewing in of inert spacer to the cut ends of the superior oblique tendon

explanation: Comments: - Brown's syndrome: SO is tight and needs to be lengthened. The most common ways to do it (in no particular order): 1. complete SO tenectomy. This frequently causes a symptomatic SO palsy (SOP), so often it is done with an IO weakening procedure (choice C). Another consideration is to try to cut the muscle fibers without cutting the tendon sheath, as the sheath will form a sort of spacer to weaken without a complete SOP (choice A).

question: Which of the following statements regarding "cyclic esotropia" is not true?

options.C: binocular function on straight days is likely
options.D: patching may convert it into constant esotropia

explanation: Cyclic esotropia is a rare form of strabismus occurring in ~1:4000 strabismus patients. It is well known for its unpredictable response to different forms of therapy EXCEPT for muscle surgery which is usually curative. Fusion is absent on strabismic days as suppression often occurs. But on "straight" days, there is binocular function. In older children who cannot develop suppression, one may get diplopic symptoms on strabismic days. Patching may convert a cyclic esotropia into a constant manifest esotropia.

question: You are operating on an elderly diabetic patient who is only allowing you to work on his right eye. He has a large-angle exotropia and right hypertropia. You plan to perform a lateral rectus recession and a medial rectus resection for his exotropia. You would also like to correct his hypertropia. Which of the following additional procedures is LEAST likely to lead to anterior segment ischemia AND treat his right hypertropia?
explanation: Anterior segment ischemia is a complication of strabismus surgery when more than 2 rectus muscles are operated in one sitting. In patients with vascular risk factors, simultaneous surgery on 3 rectus muscles may lead to this, as the blood supply to the anterior segment of the eye is provided by the anterior ciliary arteries that travel with the rectus muscles. Superior rectus recession (choice "A") or inferior rectus resection (choice "C") can treat a hypertropia, but performing either procedure would result in a total of three rectus muscles being operated on. To avoid operating on a third rectus muscle, one can turn to the oblique muscles. Superior oblique tenotomy (choice "B") weakens the superior oblique and would further worsen the hypertropia. Thus, the most appropriate procedure to treat this patient's hypertropia would be an inferior oblique myectomy (choice "D") which weakens the inferior oblique. Another solution to avoid anterior segment ischemia is to perform staged surgery. Sometimes, one can also get an iris angiogram to evaluate the circulation of the anterior segment prior to operating on the third or fourth rectus muscle.

question: A 60-year old diabetic patient presents with a left CN VI palsy. You are contemplating injecting his left medial rectus muscle with botulinum toxin type A (i.e. BoTox). The patient asks you how long the BoTox injection will paralyze his medial rectus muscle and what effect it will have on this muscle. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?
explanation: BoTox injection usually paralyzes the muscle starting approximately 2-4 days after injection. It results in muscle *lengthening* with an effect lasting 5 to 8 weeks. This is in contrast to its duration when injected into the orbicularis muscle (e.g. for blepharospasm) where it lasts 3 or more months. Comments: - Botox is also used for removing the appearance of wrinkles--if it contracted muscles it would make wrinkles worse. So it must lengthen muscles.

explanation: Comments: - You need at least 10 prism diopters for a difference deciding between A and V, V pattern... V is 5 in roman numerals...

explanation:
In contrast, an "A pattern" is considered clinically significant when the measured

question: Manipulation of which of the following extraocular muscles is most likely to result in the oculocardiac reflex?

options.C: lateral rectus resection on the uninvolved side

explanation: Manipulation of the extraocular muscles can result in bradycardia and even asystole. If there is great concern for this complication, intravenous atropine can be given. Obviously, grasping of the muscle should be released if the patient experiences this complication in the O.R.

question: Which of the following most likely describes her condition?
explanation: Patients who have spasm of the near reflex present with excessive convergence, accommodation, and miosis. These patients have normal ductions (e.g. one eye covered), but an abduction deficit on version eye movements (i.e. when both eyes open). Spasm of the near reflex is also known as "ciliary spasm" or "convergence spasm." The cause of this acquired, non-accommodative esotropia is thought to be functional (e.g. related to stress and anxiety). These patients present with acute esotropia that alternates with being orthotropic. They often have myopia on manifest, but if cyclopleged, have no significant myopia or no additional myopia beyond their baseline refraction. The treatment of spasm of the near reflex includes: • Identifying and addressing causative factors (e.g. emotional stress/anxiety) • Cycloplegic agents (e.g. atropine) • Hyperopic correction (if patient is significantly hyperopic) • Bifocals (to help with the excessive accommodation) • Rarely: botulinum injections of the medial rectus muscles and/or strabismus surgery (only if the spasm cannot be broken)

question: Which of the following tests can be used to identify opacities in the visual axis as well as to detect ocular misalignment?
explanation: The Bruckner test is performed by shining a direct ophthalmoscope into both eyes to elicit a red reflex in both eyes simultaneously. It tests for bifoveal fixation and the performer is looking for asymmetry of the red reflex. There are many etiologies to why the red reflex is asymmetrical, from lens opacities, to strabismus, to even anisometropia. This test is done mostly by primary care physicians to grossly detect strabismus or lens opacities, but it is also useful for ophthalmologists. One looks for the brightness of the red reflex. If the red reflex is dim in one eye and bright in the other eye, then one can be suspicious that the brighter eye has strabismus. This is due to foveation of the ophthalmoscope filament dims the red reflex, so the brighter reflex eye is actually the strabismic eye. The Hirschberg test is performed by shining a light (with a penlight) onto both eyes and looking at the corneal light reflex. This is a very rough estimate of ocular deviation by observing the the decentration of the corneal light reflection. If the light reflex is in the center of the pupil, then it is normal; if the reflex is at the edge of the pupil (pupillary margin), then it is 30 PD; if the reflex is in the middle of the iris, it is 60 PD; and if it is at the limbus, then 90 PD. The Krimsky test uses prisms to quantify the decentration of the corneal reflex. So it is like a Hirshberg in that one shines a direct ophthalmoscope into both eyes and looks at the corneal light reflex, but rather than estimating the decentration, one holds a prism over either eye and slides the prism bar or adjusts the prism power to center the corneal light reflex symmetrically in each eye. The Hirschberg test is used for the uncooperative patient who will not allow you to approach or use a prism to get a strabismus measurement. The Krimsky test is useful if there is poor fixation in one eye (due to dense amblyopia, low vision, blindness, etc) to allow for cover-uncover testing and strabismus measurement.

question: You are examining a patient who presents with a left hypertropia. On left gaze, you note that the right eye has deficient elevation. Which of the following is INCORRECT in distinguishing inferior oblique palsy from Brown's syndrome?

options.A: negative forced ductions in inferior oblique palsy
options.B: V pattern is present in inferior oblique palsy
options.C: superior oblique overaction is usually present
options.D: there is intorsion of the right eye

explanation: Both Brown's syndrome and inferior oblique palsy will present with deficient elevation in adduction. However, the following characterize Brown syndrome: (a) positive forced duction testing; (b) V pattern; (c) none or minimal superior oblique muscle overaction; (d) no torsion; (e) negative head tilt test Inferior oblique palsy is characterized by: (a) negative forced ductions; (b) A pattern; (c) superior oblique muscle overaction; (d) intorsion; (e) positive head-tilt test The way to think about Brown syndrome is that it is a failure of elevation in adduction due to a restriction from the trochlea-superior oblique (SO) complex. So the affected eye cannot move up and in because of this trochlea restriction, so in upgaze in a Brown patient, one gets a divergence pattern (the affected eye cannot move in so it moves out), hence a V-pattern. The superior oblique muscle is fine in Brown syndrome so there is no over-action or under-action of the muscle versus in an inferior oblique palsy, there is often secondary superior oblique muscle over-action. The secondary superior oblique muscle over-action leads to the A pattern, the intorsion of the eye, and the positive tilt test. The restriction from the trochlea-SO complex is also what gives the positive forced auction test in Brown syndrome.

question: In which of the following patients with strabismus would chemodenervation with botulinum toxin be the LEAST useful?
explanation: Chemodenervation has been shown to be most effective in small- to moderate-angle esotropia and exotropia (<40PD), posterior residual strabismus (2-8 weeks following surgery or later), acute paralytic strabismus (especially sixth cranial nerve palsy) for elimination of diplopia symptoms while the palsy recovers, active thyroid disease when surgery is inappropriate/no stabilization of the disease so there is changing motility measurements, and lastly, as a supplement to medial rectus recessions in large-angle infantile esotropia. Chemodenervation is generally not useful for patients with large deviations, "A" or "V" patterns, dissociated vertical deviations, or restrictive strabismus (e.g. due to orbital fractures).

question: Which of the following statements best defines a "-phoria"?

options.A: A manifest deviation which presents when fusional control is present part of the time
options.B: A manifest deviation which presents when fusional control is not present
options.C: A latent deviation which presents when fusional control is not present
options.D: A latent deviation which presents when fusional control is present part of the time

explanation: A -tropia is a manifest deviation that cannot be controlled by the fusional mechanism so that eyes are misaligned even under binocular conditions. Answer "A" describes an intermittent -tropia.

question: You are examining a new patient with high myopia (axial length of 28 mm OU) who complains of double vision. Which of the following extraocular muscles is NOT typically involved in patients with high myopia who have symptomatic strabismus?
explanation: In high myopes, the elongated globe can herniate between the superior and lateral recti. Imaging studies have demonstrated stretching and dehiscence of the intermuscular septum between these two muscles. High myopia can also cause inferior slippage o the lateral rectus pulley. These changes can result in a progressively worsening hypotropia and esotropia. Also, the medial rectus is frequently tight which can worsen the esotropia. This is also called "heavy eye syndrome". Management of these patients include prisms, and surgical intervention will need to address the lateral rectus muscle slippage by joining the superior and lateral rectus muscle with a loop myopexy to reposition the globe. Recession of the medial rectus muscle may also be needed if that muscle is tight. Comments: - somebody needs to discuss the difference between heavy eye syndrome and sagging eye syndrome - Sagging eye syndrome is different from heavy eye syndrome in that "heavy eye syndrome" is reserved for patients with high myopia and axial elongation resulting in the globe prolapsing superotemporally. "Sagging eye syndrome" is describing elderly patients who have esotropia more at distance than near due to the degeneration of the pulley system in the orbit.

question: After you place a 4-PD base-out prism over a 4-year-old boy's right eye, you observe abduction of the left eye. You then place the same 4-PD base-out prism over his left eye, and you observe no movement of either eye. What condition does this boy have?

options.B: He has amblyopia of the right eye

explanation: This is a 4-PD base-out test. A normal response is when you place the 4-PD prism base-out over either eye, you will observe a movement of the uncovered eye away from the covered eye, followed by a convergence of the uncovered eye towards the covered eye. Hence, it is an abduction movement followed by an adduction movement. For example, you place the 4-PD BO over the left eye, you will see the right eye abduct (Herring's law) followed by the right eye adducting (convergence). In this question, when you place the prism in front of a fixating eye, and you observe a movement away from the fixating eye BUT NO convergence response, this suggests that there is a suppression scotoma. This is because the nonfixating eye does not "see" the image because it has fallen into the scotoma. Thus, this patient has monofixation syndrome.

question: All of the following represent possible surgical corrections of strabismus caused by cranial nerve III palsy EXCEPT:

options.A: large lateral rectus recession with large medial rectus resection with supraplacement of both
options.B: disinsertion of lateral rectus with reattachment to the orbital periosteum
options.C: large lateral rectus recession with fixation of the globe to the lateral orbital periosteum

explanation: Fixation of the globe to the lateral orbital periosteum would exacerbate exotropia. Instead, lateral rectus recession combined with fixation of the globe to the *nasal* orbital periosteum could be performed.

question: Which of the following is FALSE regarding Duane's syndrome?

options.A: it can be associated with systemic syndromes like Goldenhar syndrome
options.B: it is thought to be caused by a defect in development during the 4th week of gestation
options.C: in most anatomical and imaging studies, the nucleus of the third cranial nerve is absent
options.D: it can be characterized by globe retraction during adduction

explanation: Actually, most imaging and anatomical studies have shown that the nucleus of the 6th cranial nerve is absent (not third cranial nerve). In addition, there is typically an aberrant branch of the 3rd cranial nerve that innervates the lateral rectus. Please note that the BCSC Pediatrics book does NOT distinguish between the different subtypes of Duane's syndrome when talking about these neuroimaging findings.

question: You are performing strabismus surgery for a 6-year old child with exotropia. During the course of the surgery, you accidentally create a tear in Tenon's capsule such that orbital fat prolapses through. Which of the following represents the best course of management at this stage?

options.A: do not worry about the prolapsed fat since it is endogenous tissue and will have minimal consequences
options.B: immediately stop the surgery and tell the parents what happened
options.C: place a patch graft over the tear to stop additional fat from prolapsing
options.D: excise the prolapsed fat and close the tear with absorbable sutures

explanation: Prolapsed orbital fat may result in a scar that may limit motility. This is called "adherence syndrome." The best course of action is excising the prolapsed fat and closing the tear with absorbable sutures.

question: Which of the following is the treatment for isoametropic (bilateral refractive) amblyopia?

options.B: Optimal refractive correction plus alternate patch 2 hours per day (e.g. Patch right eye 2 h Monday, Wednesday, Friday; Patch left eye 2 h Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday)
options.C: Optimal refractive correction plus alternate patch 6 hours per day (e.g. Patch right eye 6 h Monday, Wednesday, Friday; Patch left eye 6 h Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday)
options.D: Optimal refractive correction plus atropine in both eyes

explanation: Isoametropic (ametropic) or bilateral refractive amblyopia can develop in children with large amounts of uncorrected hypermetropia, myopia, astigmatism or a combination of these factors in both eyes. The presumed mechanism involves pattern vision deprivation. The Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group conducted a prospective, multicenter, non- comparative intervention in 113 children < 10 years of age with bilateral refractive amblyopia.1 The patients were placed in optical spectacle correction and visual acuity measured over the course of 52 weeks. At 52 weeks, 74% had a visual acuity of 20/25 or better in both eyes. Thus, treatment involves refractive correction alone (Answer A). Because the process is bilateral, there is no need for penalization unless additional factors such as anisometropia or strabismus are present and fail to improve with glasses alone. The American Academy of Ophthalmology has developed Preferred Practice Patterns for considering refractive correction based on patient age and symptomatology (see Table below).2 1 Wallace DK, Chandler DL, Beck RW, et al. Treatment of bilateral refractive amblyopia in children three to less than 10 years of age. Am J Ophthalmol. Oct 2007;144(4):487- 496. 2 American Academy of Ophthalmology,Pediatric Ophthalmology/Strabismus Panel.Preferred Practice Pattern Guidelines. Amblyopia. San Francisco, CA: American Academy of Ophthalmology;2012. Available at:.

question: Which of the following strabismus patterns is most frequent in patients with a craniosynostosis syndrome like Apert syndrome?
explanation: Comments: - The inferior oblique overreaction is more of an "apparent overreaction" and not a true overreaction. "Coronal synostosis causes ipsilateral orbital extorsion and superior lateral orbit elongation, leading to globe extorsion with upward offset of the medial rectus and downward offset of the lateral rectus. As a result, the medial rectus behaves like an elevator in adduction, and as a corollary, the lateral rectus muscle may be acting as a depressor in abduction. This simulates inferior oblique overaction. In addition, superior orbital rim retrusion may lead to superior oblique trochlea retrusion resulting in superior oblique underaction and secondary inferior oblique overaction."--.

question: A 7-year-old patient with a history of accommodative esotropia comes into your office for an evaluation. Without spectacles, the patient has an obvious large- angle esotropia. You decide to use the Maddox rod test to quantify this deviation and place the Maddox rod in front of the left eye. Which of the following responses will the patient likely say in regards to the orientation of the lights?

options.A: The red vertical line is to the left of the white light
options.B: The red vertical line is to the right of the white light
options.C: The red horizontal line is to the left of the white light
options.D: The red horizontal line is to the right of the white light

explanation: To quantify horizontal deviations (as in the case of esotropia), you should orient the cylinders of the rod horizontally. This will produce a vertical line that is perceived by the patient. For esotropia, the red line and white light will be on the same side of their respective eyes. In this case, the rod is in front of the left eye; therefore the patient sees a red vertical line to the left of the white light that is seen by the right eye. In the case of exotropia, the line and light would be crossed (i.e. red line to the right of the white light). One can also simulate crossed and uncrossed diplopia to aid in understanding of this concept. One experiences uncrossed diplopia when one is eSotropic, and one experiences crossed diplopia when one is eXotropic. To simulate eSotropia, grab a pen in one hand and hold it in front of you with your arm extended, then place your other hand's index finger approximately half distance from your pen and your nose (ok to be closer to your nose). Focus on your index finger (this is you in convergence or eSotropia). Now your pen in the background is outside of Panum's area and should be seen as 2 separate images (one on the left and another one on the right. Don't worry if you don't see the diplopic pen yet. Now close your left eye, the pen image on the left disappears! Then open your left eye and close your right eye, the pen image on the right disappears! You have just experienced UNCROSSED diplopia from eSotropia. Similarly, to simulate eXotropia, perform the same arrangement. Now, instead of focusing on your index finger, focus on your pen to start with (this is you in divergence or eXotropia). Your index finger is outside of Panum's area and should be doubled. Again, don't worry if you don't see it yet. Now close your left eye, the index finger on the right disappears! Now open your left eye and close the right eye, the index finger on the left disappears! This is CROSSED diplopia from eXotropia. The reason for the above phenomenon is as follows: in eSotropia, the eyeball is turned inward, so the fovea is moved outward, away from the nose or temporally. An image/light that is coming in from straight ahead is going to fall nasal to the fovea (remember the fovea is moved outward or temporally in eSotropia). But then the nasal side of the retina perceives the temporal side of the visual field. So the image is perceived as coming from the temporal side of the visual field. So an eSotropic eye sees the image displaced temporally and is UNCROSSED. Now the opposite situation occurs for eXotropia. The eyeball is turned outward, so the fovea is moved inward or toward the nose or nasally. An image/light coming from straight ahead is falling temporal to the fovea (again, remember the fovea is now inward or nasal), and thus the perceived image is the nasal side of the visual field. So in eXotropia, the diplopia image is perceived as displaced nasally and is CROSSED (like a X). Comments: - To remember that eXotropia is "crossed", think of the letter X which is written by crossing two straight lines.

question: According to the "Amblyopia Treatment Studies" completed by the Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group, which of the following lead to improved visual acuity in patients with stable, residual amblyopia?

options.A: Addition of levodopa (0.51 mg/kg) combined with carbidopa (0.17 mg/kg tid)
options.B: Additional of levodopa (0.76 mg/kg) combined with carbidopa (0.17 mg/kg tid)
options.C: Addition of penalization with a plano lens in the sound eye of patients currently using atropine
options.D: Increased patching to 6 hours in patients previously patching 2 hours per day

explanation: In the "Amblyopia Treatment Study" (ATS) #17, 139 patients ages 7 to 12 years were randomized to either continued 2 hours of patching + placebo or 2 hours of patching + levodopa. Visual acuity improved 5.3 letters in the levodopa group and 3.8 letters in the patching group, a difference that was not statistically significant. Therefore, in this patient population studied, levodopa was not effective in leading to increased visual acuity as compared to placebo.1 Likewise in the ATS #16, 73 patients ages 3 to 8 years with stable, residual amblyopia on atropine treatment in the sound eye were randomized to continuation of atropine alone versus augmentation with plano lenses. The visual acuity improved 0.6 lines in the atropine-only group and 1.1 lines in the atropine + plano lens, a difference that was not statistically significant.2 Of note, the confidence interval was large, and thus a larger population is needed to truly determine treatment effect. In ATS #15, 169 patients ages 3 to < 8 years with stable, residual amblyopia currently patching 2 hours/day were randomized to either escalated treatment of 6 hours of patching/day or maintaining 2 hours/day. At 12 weeks, visual acuity improved 1.2 lines in the 6 hour group and 0.5 lines in the 2 hour group, a difference that was statistically significant.3 Therefore of the answer choices, a well-designed randomized study has found prescribing increased patching from 2 to 6 hours to be effective in the treatment of residual, stable amblyopia. References: 1 Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator G, Repka MX, Kraker RT, et al. A randomized trial of levodopa as treatment for residual amblyopia in older children. Ophthalmology. May 2015;122(5):874-881. 2 Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator G, Wallace DK, Lazar EL, et al. A randomized trial of adding a plano lens to atropine for amblyopia. J Aapos. Feb 2015;19(1):42-48. 3 Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator G, Wallace DK, Lazar EL, et al. A randomized trial of increasing patching for amblyopia. Ophthalmology. Nov 2013;120(11):. Comments: - What is considered "Stable" amblyopia? - No improvement or further improvement in visual acuity for 12 weeks with patching 2 hours/day.

question: What is the most likely cause of this child's esotropia?
explanation: This child developed an esotropia during the patching of one of his eyes (i.e. artificial disruption of binocular vision). The esotropia is comitant and not associated with a significant amount of hyperopia. This is the definition of "basic acquired non accommodative esotropia." Acquired esotropia may be acute in onset and are commonly associated with symptoms of diplopia. The child has full ductions so CN VI palsy is unlikely. He also has negligible hyperopia thus making refractive accommodative esotropia also not the diagnosis. Sensory esotropia results from monocular vision loss but the vision loss needs to be significant, such as from a congenital cataract or optic nerve disease.

question: Which of the following is used as amblyopia therapy?
explanation: Bangerter foils are a system of graded foils that are fit adhesively to glasses, much like Fresnel prisms. Foils are available in various levels of opacification (i.e. like neutral density filters), allowing the provider to control the level of blur in the non-amblyopic eye. These are used with variable frequency among pediatric providers, but are potentially useful tools in patients with mild/moderate amblyopia who are intolerant of patching or atropine penalization.

question: You are examining a 2-year old child who appears to have an intermittent esotropia at near. What is the accurate abbreviation to describe this patient's deviation?
explanation: "E" indicates an esophoria. E(T) indicates an intermittent esotropia. Adding a prime symbol to any of the notations indicates near fixation. In this case, E'(T) indicates intermittent esotropia at near fixation.

question: All of the following are characteristic of bilateral vs. unilateral superior oblique palsy EXCEPT:

options.A: unilateral cases usually demonstrate little if any V pattern
options.B: unilateral cases usually have at least 15 degrees of excyclotorsion
options.C: in bilateral cases, there is right hypertropia on right head tilt and left hypertropia on left head tilt
options.D: bilateral cases usually have more than 10 degrees of excyclotorsion

explanation: Unilateral cases usually have no (or minimal) V-pattern associated with it. There is also typically less than 5 degrees of excyclotorsion with unilateral cases compared to more than 10 degrees for bilateral cases.

question: All of the following statements regarding cranial nerve VI palsy in children is true EXCEPT:

options.A: A face-turn is protective against amblyopia in the affected eye
options.B: Neuro-imaging is indicated in many of these children presenting with this palsy
options.C: Most cases of suspected congenital CN VI palsy actually represent congenital esotropia with cross fixation
options.D: CN VI palsy occurs more frequently in infants than in older children

explanation: CN VI palsy is much more common in older children compared to at birth or during infancy. For these patients, a face-turn is protective against amblyopia since this will produce a single binocular image. As many as 1/3 of these patients will have an underlying intracranial lesion that requires neuro-imaging. It is important to check ductions in infants suspected of congenital CN VI palsy since, in the majority of cases, the child usually has congenital esotropia with cross-fixation simulating the abduction deficit.

question: What exam finding allows differentiation between bilateral primary oblique overaction versus bilateral paralysis of the antagonist oblique muscle?

options.A: Subjective torsion on double Maddox rod testing
options.C: Up and down gaze discrepancy of >10 prism diopters

explanation: The main differential diagnosis between primary oblique overaction and palsy of the antagonist oblique muscle is settled with the head tilt test. With bilateral superior oblique palsy, head tilt test should reveal alternating hypertropias (i.e. right hypertropia on right tilt; left hypertropia on left tilt). In primary oblique dysfunction, the difference in vertical deviation with head tilt is minimal. A patient with significant inferior oblique overaction may be expected to have small to negligible hypertropia on right and left head tilt. Here is an explanation for the head tilt test: in the Parks Bielshowsky 3-step test, when the head is tilted to the right, the right eye is intorted and the left eye is extorted to compensate for the head tilt. Therefore, the RSO and the LIO are most at function. Similarly, when the head is tilted left, the right eye is extorted and the left eye is intorted to compensate for the left head tilt, and hence the RIO and LSO are at work. In a left superior oblique palsy with secondary inferior oblique overaction, one will see the LSO weak on left tilt, and LIO stronger on right tilt. If one has a primary inferior oblique overaction, one would see LIO stronger on right tilt but no LSO weakness on left tilt. So in a bilateral superior oblique palsy with bilateral secondary inferior oblique overaction case, on right tilt, one has RSO weak plus LIO strong (LIO strong from LSO palsy) = big hyper; on left tilt, one has LSO weak plus RIO strong (RIO strong from RSO palsy) = big hyper. But in a primary inferior oblique overreaction, on right tilt, just LIO strong = small hyper, on left tilt, just RIO strong = small hyper. Subjective torsion may not be present as the patient may develop sensory adaptations. Typically, objective extorsion of the fundus is seen in inferior oblique overaction and intorsion in superior oblique overaction. The discrepancy in up and down gaze of > 10 PD indicates a pattern strabismus and can suggest either inferior oblique or superior oblique overreaction, but it cannot distinguish primary versus secondary causes. Additionally, it is rare for bilateral superior oblique overaction to be secondary to inferior oblique palsy, as primary inferior oblique palsies exist seldomly. If superior oblique overaction is bilateral and symmetric, there will be no hypertropia in primary position, but there will be an ‘A’ pattern. Large vertical fusional amplitudes can be used to distinguish a congenital case of superior oblique palsy versus an acquired case.

question: Which of the following is not a cause of over-elevation in adduction in cases of incomitant vertical deviations?
explanation: Incomitant vertical deviations commonly feature a hypertropia that is worse on gaze to one side. They are often associated with oblique muscle abnormalities. This is mostly observed as over-elevations or over-depressions in ADDuction, as the superior oblique and inferior oblique actions are more isolated in those gaze positions (remember cardinal positions). Some causes of over-elevation in adduction are inferior oblique muscle overreaction, often due to superior oblique palsy. Dissociated vertical deviation (DVD) can also cause this because the line-of-sight of the involved eye is blocked by the nose so the DVD becomes apparent. Large-angle exotropia commonly has a vertical component. Orbital dysmorphism or craniofacial syndromes usually has superior oblique palsy/inferior oblique overreaction. Brown syndrome is, by definition, failure of elevation in ADDuction; hence, one would see over-depression in adduction and not over-elevation in adduction.

question: A 40-year old man presents to your office complaining of long-standing diplopia. He also complains that "everything seems to oscillate" even when he closes his left eye. All of the following are appropriate interventions for this symptomatic disturbance EXCEPT:

options.C: superior oblique tenectomy with simultaneous inferior oblique weakening

explanation: This vignette describes monocular "oscillopsia" that occurs from superior oblique myokymia. In superior oblique myokymia, there are torsional movements of the involved eye in an otherwise neurogically-normal individual. Treatment includes systemic medications like carbamazepine and phenytoin as well as topical timolol. Surgical correction consists of superior oblique tenectomy with simultaneous inferior oblique weakening. Harada-Ito is a procedure marked by advancement (or strengthening) of the anterior fibers of the superior oblique tendon that are most responsible for ocular torsion. This is useful in patients with a 4th nerve palsy manifesting with significant excyclotorsion but without significant ipsilateral hypertropia. It is a surgical procedure to correct excyclotorsion with limited effect on vertical alignment. NYSTAGMUS/DIPLOPIA.

question: You are having difficulty estimating the visual acuity of a preverbal 1-year-old child who has had horizontal nystagmus since birth. On exam, you note a left jerk nystagmus which worsens on left gaze and dampens on right gaze. How would you properly estimate this child's visual acuity with an optokinetic nystagmus (OKN) drum?

options.A: rotate the OKN drum to the child's left
options.B: rotate the OKN drum to the child's right
options.C: rotate the OKN upwards or downwards
options.D: rotate the OKN to the child's right for a moment and then quickly to the child's left

explanation: In children with horizontal nystagmus, it may be difficult to see this endpoint reflex if the drum is rotated horizontally. This is because the reflex may be hidden by the already- abnormal horizontal movements. In this case, it is more proper to rotate the OKN drum vertically and to see if a vertical nystagmus reflex movement occurs. If such a vertical reflex occurs, the child's visual acuity is usually 20/400 or better.

question: Which of the following conditions is classically associated with "dissociated nystagmus?"
explanation: "Dissociated nystagmus" describes when the nystagmus only occurs in the abducting eye. The classic example of this abnormal eye movement is found in internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO). There is debate whether this movement is a true nystagmus or instead, a series of saccades. As you probably know, INO is typically caused by either demyelination or stroke resulting in disruption of the ipsilateral medial longitudinal fasciculus. Other possible causes of dissociated nystagmus include myasthenia gravis and following surgical weakening of one eye's medial rectus muscle. Comments: - Dissociated Nystagmus: "occurs when the amplitude of oscillations differs in each eye" per Neuro text, so not just when you only have nystagmus in the ABducting eye. There is another question that asks to pair the term with this correct description.

question: For children with congenital sensory nystagmus, which order of eye movements is typically associated with the worst to best visual acuity?

options.A: searching nystagmus < pendular nystagmus < jerk nystagmus
options.B: searching nystagmus < jerk nystagmus < pendular nystagmus
options.C: pendular nystagmus < searching nystagmus < jerk nystagmus
options.D: pendular nystagmus < jerk nystagmus < searching nystagmus

explanation: The pendular pattern is the most common, and it typically occurs when the visual acuity is at least 20/200 in at least 1 eye. Jerk nystagmus is associated with the best visual acuity (~20/60 to 20/100) while searching nystagmus typically occurs when visual acuity is worse than 20/200. CORNEAL ABNORMALITIES.

question: All of the following are true regarding sclerocornea EXCEPT:

options.A: the corneal opacity is generally greater peripherally rather than centrally
options.B: the cornea is generally steeper than normal eyes
options.C: it is often associated with systemic abnormalities
options.D: there generally is no apparent scleral sulcus

explanation: Sclerocornea can be differentiated from Peter's anomaly because the cornea is generally clearer centrally in sclerocornea while the central cornea is more opaque in Peter's anomaly. The cornea in sclerocornea is generally flatter than normal (not steeper). The other components of the mnemonic are: • T: trauma/tears in Descemet's membrane • U: ulcer (e.g. bacterial) • M: metabolic conditions (e.g. mucopolysaccharidoses like Hurler syndrome) • P: posterior corneal defect (e.g. Peter's) • E: endothelial defect (e.g. CHED) • D: dermoid.

question: Among the following diseases, which is associated with the greatest frequency and severity of corneal clouding?
explanation: Scheie syndrome is an inherited disease of metabolism in which the body cannot properly break down long chains of sugar molecules called glycosaminoglycans. The syndrome belongs to a group of diseases called mucopolysaccharidoses (MPS). The enzyme defect in Scheie syndrome is of lysosomal alpha-L-iduronidase. Scheie syndrome is actually the mildest form of MPS type 1 which also includes the entities Hurler syndrome and Hurler-Scheie syndrome. MPS type 2 is equivalent to Hunter syndrome whose major ophthalmic sign is retinal degeneration. All of the syndromes listed, besides Scheie syndrome, do not feature corneal clouding as part of their stigmata. GLAUCOMA.

question: One of your long-term patients with a history of congenital glaucoma is planning on starting a family. He is worried about his kids developing this ocular disease because it was "horrible growing up visually-handicapped." Besides himself, there are no other family members (including his wife) affected by congenital glaucoma. What is the percentage chance that his son or daughter will develop congenital glaucoma?
explanation: If there is no family history of congenital glaucoma, then an affected parent has an approximately 2% chance of having an affected child with this ocular disease. This risk calculation is based on a retrospective study performed in Australia.1 For all of you naysayers, this is verbatim what the BCSC Pediatrics book states: "When no other family history of PCG [primary congenital glaucoma] exists, the chance of an affected parent having an affected child is approximately 2%." Please review the source article if you still have doubts. 1Hewitt AW, MacKinnon JR, Giubilato A, Elder JE, Craig JE, Mackey DA. Familial transmission risk of infantile glaucoma in Australia. Ophthalmic Genet. 2006;27:93-7.

question: You are performing an examination under anesthesia for a 1-month-old child who you suspect has primary congenital glaucoma. What is the normal cup-to- disc ratio of normal newborn eyes?
explanation: According to the BCSC, most normal newborn eyes have cup-to-disc ratios of less than 0.3. In addition, there is usually less than 0.2 difference between the cup-to-disc ratios between the two eyes of a child. As you probably know, "reversal of cupping" is a phenomenon that may occur after a child with congenital glaucoma is adequately treated with glaucoma surgery. After significant lowering of intraocular pressure, the magnitude of cupping may decrease dramatically in these patients.

question: Which of the following is TRUE regarding those individuals affected by primary congenital glaucoma (PCG)?

options.A: PCG is equally common among males and females
options.B: PCG is typically diagnosed at birth
options.C: PCG results in blindness in 40-75% of cases
options.D: PCG is bilateral in approximately two-thirds of cases

explanation: PCG results in blindness in approximately 5-15% of affected individuals (not 40- 75%). It occurs more frequently in males (66%) compared to females (33%). It is typically diagnosed within the first year of life, but usually not at birth. If PCG is diagnosed after age 5, then it is technically called juvenile open-angle glaucoma. PCG affects both eyes in approximately two-thirds of affected individuals.

question: In which of the following patients would the risk of aphakic glaucoma be highest?

options.A: 10-year-old child with megalocornea who underwent cataract surgery at age 1 year
options.B: 10-year-old child with megalocornea who underwent cataract surgery at age 8 years
options.C: 10-year-old child with microcornea who underwent cataract surgery at age 1 year
options.D: 10-year-old child with microcornea who underwent cataract surgery at age 8 years

explanation: Aphakic glaucoma occurs more frequently in those children who had cataract surgery during infancy. The risk is considered highest in children with microcornea. Other risk factors for the development of aphakic glaucoma: • Cataract surgery in the first year of life • post-operative complications.

question: What is the mean NORMAL intraocular pressure (IOP) of a newborn child?
explanation: Infants with primary congenital glaucoma often have IOPs in the 30 to 40 mmHg range, and may still have IOPs in the 20 mmHg range under general anesthesia. IRIS ABNORMALITIES.

question: A 6-year-old child is referred to your office after his pediatrician noticed "something strange about his right eye." On slit-lamp examination, you note the iris abnormality seen in the photo above (see arrow). This finding is confined to the right eye; his left eye appears completely normal. His intraocular pressures are 35 and 10 mmHg in the right and left eyes respectively. Which of the following abnormalities might this child also display given his most likely ocular diagnosis?
explanation: The slit-lamp photo demonstrates an eye with ectropion uveae which is actually a misnomer since the iris posterior epithelium is not considered part of the uvea. An alternative name is iris ectropion. This abnormality can occur either as an acquired tractional abnormality (e.g. from neovascularization of the iris) or can be congenital in origin (i.e. congenital iris ectropion). The constellation of unilateral congenital iris ectropion, high iris insertion, smooth (cryptless) iris surface, and glaucoma is called congenital iris ectropion syndrome. This syndrome may be associated with systemic syndromes like neurofibromatosis (NF), primary facial hemihypertrophy, Rieger anomaly, and Prader- Willi syndrome. Café au lait spots are common cutaneous manifestations of NF. "Adenoma sebaceum" is also a misnomer for the facial angiofibromas (which appear as red papules) that occur in individuals with tuberous sclerosis. Nevus of Ota is the blue facial hyperpigmentation that occurs in individuals with oculodermal melanocytosis. Some individuals with iris mammillations can also have oculodermal melanocytosis. Dilated cardiomyopathy is one of the systemic manifestations of Alström syndrome. This very rare genetic disorder features a cone-rod dystrophy leading to early blindness as its ocular manifestation. Comments: - I may be wrong, but I believe the iris is considered to be part of the uvea (iris, ciliary body, choroid). - I think the author was referring to the posterior aspect of the iris, which has neuroectodermal origin and is an extension of the retina.

question: A 2-year-old infant is referred to you for an "iris mass." After a thorough examination under anesthesia including ultrasound biomicroscopy, you diagnose the infant with an iris stromal cyst. This cyst is completely obstructing the visual axis. Which of the following is the preferred management choice?
explanation: Unlike other iris cysts of childhood (e.g. primary pigment epithelial cysts) which typically require no treatment, iris stromal cysts can enlarge rapidly and be associated with blockage of the visual axis, corneal decompensation (from corneal touch), glaucoma, and uveitis due to leakage of cyst contents. Observation is not the preferred management choice if the cyst is obstructing the visual axis due to the risk of deprivational amblyopia. Of the remaining management choices, surgical excision is currently the preferred treatment modality (according to the BCSC) due to the increased recurrence rates of the other listed modalities.

question: You are examining a 10-year-old girl who was referred by her pediatrician for "heterochromia." On slit-lamp exam, you note multiple iris nodules as seen in the photo above. This abnormality is only seen in this child's right eye. There are no corneal abnormalities. What other abnormality is associated with this iris abnormality?
explanation: The slit lamp photo shows diffuse, smooth protuberances of the anterior iris surface. Importantly, these nodules are of the same color as the surrounding iris. These features are characteristic of iris mammillations. Iris mammillations are more commonly found in dark eyes and can occur in an unilateral or bilateral fashion. It can occur in association with oculodermal melanocytosis and "phakomatosis pigmentovascularis type IIb." In addition, there are case reports of its association with ciliary body and choroidal melanoma. The differential diagnosis of iris mammillations includes: Lisch nodules, ocular and oculodermal melanocytosis, malignant melanoma of the iris, Cogan-Reese syndrome, and iris granulomas. Unlike Lisch nodules which are a different color than the surrounding iris, mammillations are of the same color. In addition Lisch nodules are not diffusely-distributed but instead tend to be more concentrated in the inferior iris. The entities that comprise the "ICE syndrome" (i.e. Cogan-Reese, Chandler, and essential iris atrophy) all share an abnormal corneal endothelium (i.e. "beaten-bronze" appearance). The question segment specifically states that the cornea is normal; thus, this patient does not have Cogan-Reese syndrome. Also, the ICE syndrome typically occurs in adult women (not young children). Answer choice "A" is a characteristic of juvenile xanthogranuloma; choice "B" is a characteristic of Cogan-Reese syndrome; and choice "C" is a characteristic of neurofibromatosis type 1.

question: A 5-year-old child is referred to you for "small pupils." On exam, the child's pupils are small and displaced superotemporally OU. You also note that both his crystalline lenses are subluxed. Given a tentative diagnosis of "ectopia lentis et pupillae," in which direction would his lenses be displaced?
explanation: Ectopia lentis et pupillae is an asymmetric, bilateral condition in which the lens subluxation is in the opposite direction of the eccentric pupils. Therefore in this example, the lenses would be subluxed inferonasally. This condition is often said to be inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion, though there is some evidence that it can also be inherited in an autosomal dominant with reduced penetrance pattern1. Other associated ocular findings include: poor pupillary dilation, persistent pupillary membrane, iris transillumination defects, early cataract, glaucoma, high myopia, and retinal detachment. CATARACT/LENS DISORDERS.

question: What is the typical mode of inheritance of hereditary cataracts?
explanation: Another helpful fact regarding pediatric cataracts is that congenital cataracts associated with systemic diseases are ALWAYS bilateral, but bilaterality does NOT ensure that an underyling systemic disorder is the cause.

question: What types of congenital cataracts are associated with this child's most likely systemic disorder?
explanation: Lowe syndrome is a very rare, X-linked disease with an estimated prevalence of 1 to 10 affected males in 1 million people. It is caused by a reduction of phosphatidylinositol (4,5) bisphosphate 5 phosphatase activity below 10% in fibroblasts. The ocular findings in Lowe syndrome are dense cataracts in all patients (disciform [membranous] cataracts), glaucoma in 50% of patients (usually developing during the 1st year of life), and corneal and conjunctival keloids (25% of patients). Typically, severe hypotonia is present at birth which may compromise suction and result in severe respiratory problems during early life. Approximately 10% will have mild intellectual disability while the majority (>75%) will display overaggressive behavior. The kidney problems in Lowe syndrome is due to renal Fanconi syndrome which results in renal tubular acidosis, proteinuria, phosphate wasting, hypercalciuria, aminoaciduria, and hypokalemia. These renal abnormalities result in failure to thrive and rickets. Anterior subcapsular cataracts are associated with lens trauma (e.g. implantable collamer lens placement) and atopic dermatitis. Cerulean ("blue-dot") cataracts are bilateral, small, bluish-white opacities in the peripheral cortex. They are typically asymptomatic and can be associated with Down's syndrome, but can also be found in normal individuals during puberty.

question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding cataracts associated with posterior lenticonus in children?

options.B: These cataracts are not present at birth
options.C: These cataracts are commonly associated with Alport syndrome
options.D: These cataracts are associated with microphthalmos

explanation: Posterior lenticonus is an outpouching of the central posterior capsule due to thinning in that area. It leads to an "oil droplet" appearance on retroillumination. Eventually, this outpouching will opacify and can even lead to complete opacification of the lens if the posterior capsule tears. These cataracts are typically unilateral, acquired (i.e. not present at birth), and are not associated with differences in size between the two eyes. Anterior lenticonus (i.e. protrusion of the anterior lens) is commonly associated with Alport syndrome (~25% of cases). Posterior lenticonus occurs only rarely in Alport syndrome (i.e. case reports). Systemic manifestations of Alport syndrome include glomerulonephritis (e.g. presenting with hematuria) and high-tone deafness. Another characteristic ocular finding in Alport syndrome is dot-and-fleck retinopathy (>80% of those affected). UVEITIS.

question: You are managing a recalcitrant case of intermediate uveitis in a 7-year-old child. You have decided to ramp up therapy and use a systemic immunosuppressive. Of the following choices, which of the immunosuppressives is generally discouraged in children?
explanation: The alkylating immunosuppressives (i.e. cyclophosphamide and chlorambucil) are generally not used in children due to the risks of bone marrow suppression, future infertility, infection, and secondary malignancies. If used, they are typically reserved for the most severe cases of uveitis. Another side effect of cyclophosphamide found on board exams is hemorrhagic cystitis. Methotrexate is a commonly used immunosuppressive that is used to treat both uveitis and arthritis in children (e.g. juvenile idiopathic arthritis). Its most common side effect is GI upset while its more serious adverse effects include ulcerative stomatitis, hepatoxicity, and pneumonitis. Common side effects of cyclosporine include gingival hyperplasia, GI upset, and renal dysfunction. In fact, renal toxicity is the main limiting factor in using cyclosporine. RETINA.

question: You are called to the NICU to examine a child with possible retinopathy of prematurity. Which dilation drop is routinely recommended for patients in this age group?
